new_statements.rule_in_words: For Gipuzkoan Basque (the dialect of all his examples, fn. 2 p. 61) de Rijk declines to give a stress rule: the system of stress assignment is unknown, varies village to village, and stressed syllables have very little acoustic prominence; he quotes Michelena (Fonética Histórica Vasca ch. 20, p. 379) that in the central and western dialects intensity/pitch/duration differences are small and the distinctive value of the accent is reduced. The one regularity he asserts: relativized finite verb forms (zutén liburua, zetorrén gizona, dutén, datorrén) take final stress as a rule, not because of the underlying -n+n cluster; non-relativized forms sometimes also get final stress, so intonation is not a foolproof marker of relativization. Fn. 4 (p. 62) speculates that final stress was originally limited to past-tense relativized forms and spread to present-tense forms by analogy. 'Guipúzcoan' normalises the scanned garble 'Guiptzcoan'; 'ocasionally' is as printed/scanned.
new_statements.exceptions: relativized verb forms occasionally lack the expected final stress; non-relativized verb forms frequently also take final stress; strong village-to-village variation; low acoustic prominence of stress generally

new_statements.quote: Hualde (1996) argues for an example in the Basque dialect of Ondarroa. [...] Phrasal accents normally are assigned to the penultimate syllable of the phrase. There is a distinction between accented and unaccented roots in Ondarroa Basque, and the accents of accented roots normally fall on the penult syllable of the word, with affixal vowels like the determiner /-a/ counting to define which is the penult: (47) /'indarr-a/ ⟶ [inddárra] 'the bean' [...] However, when the word-final vowel is deleted in hiatus, it's the surface penult (underlying antepenult) vowel of accented words that gets the word accent: (48) /'eskola-a/ ⟶ [eskóli] 'the school'

new_statements.rule_in_words: Literature-based rule for Standard Basque (Batua), after Aurrekoetxea et al. 2015 and Hualde & Elordieta 2014: no lexically contrastive accent; stress on the second syllable from the left by default; in bi- and trisyllables a heavy final syllable (diphthong or closed: limói, balkói, esán) takes the stress, otherwise the final syllable is extrametrical, so light disyllables are initial-stressed (érre) and etxéa, ikúsi are second-syllable; whole words (not roots) are the accentual unit; downstep at phrase level. The thesis's own production data (6 Bilbao-area Basque-Spanish bilinguals, words in isolation) only partly bear this out: light-light disyllables vary freely between initial and second-syllable stress within and across speakers, LH disyllables are uniformly final(=second)-stressed, three speakers (1, 5, 6) put the F0 peak on the first syllable of trisyllables (líburu, kókapen) while all lengthen the second syllable, and suffixed forms fall back to the expected second syllable.

readall_conflicts: No two opened works state opposite placements, but the sources describe different systems for different varieties: the catalog (Gordon) codes Basque as fixed second-syllable stress; de Rijk 1972 says for Gipuzkoan that no stress-assignment rule is known, prominence is weak, and relativized verb forms take final stress; the Thomas 2020 abstract says Bilbao-area Standard Basque has no contrastive word stress and its realization depends on syllable weight and count; the Ito 2002 abstract treats Bermeo (Northern Bizkaian) Basque as a lexical pitch accent language; the existing Hualde 1997 statement gives penultimate stress with lexical oxytones for the eastern dialects. None of the eight works opened here confirms the catalog's '010..' rule directly, and none refutes it; the single-rule coding masks a well-documented dialect split (predictable low-prominence stress in the centre/standard vs. lexical pitch accent in Northern Bizkaia vs. penultimate in the east). No source opened contradicts the catalog's penultimate placement. sources.quote: in NBB, there is a lexical contrast between accented and unaccented words, like in Tokyo Japanese. [...] In the particular variety of NBB on which we will base our analysis (the one of Lekeitio), main prosodic prominence is always found on a fixed syllable in an accented word, regardless of the location of that syllable with respect to the accented morpheme. This syllable is the penultimate of the whole word, which may consist of a bare root with no overt affix or a root plus one or more affixes. A falling accent HL surfaces on this penult syllable.

sources.quote: Hualde (1996) argues for an example in the Basque dialect of Ondarroa. [...] Phrasal accents normally are assigned to the penultimate syllable of the phrase. However, when the underlying phrase-final vowel has been deleted in hiatus, the final vowel of the phrase has the phrasal accent: (46) /gure abare-a/ ⟶ [gure abarí] 'our priest' [...] Word-level accent behaves differently, though. There is a distinction between accented and unaccented roots in Ondarroa Basque, and the accents of accented roots normally fall on the penult syllable of the word, with affixal vowels like the determiner /-a/ counting to define which is the penult: (47) /'indarr-a/ ⟶ [inddárra] 'the bean' [...] However, when the word-final vowel is deleted in hiatus, it's the surface penult (underlying antepenult) vowel of accented words that gets the word accent: (48) /'eskola-a/ ⟶ [eskóli] 'the school'
